Where it began

Glenn Maxwell was born in Kew, Victoria, on 14 October 1988, and learned the game at South Belgrave Cricket Club. He started out bowling medium pace before switching to off-spin as a boy. Victoria first took him into their squad in 2009–10.

The country noticed him in February 2011, when he hit 51 from 19 balls against Tasmania, at the time the quickest fifty in Australian domestic one-day cricket. Within weeks he had made his first-class debut, and a first hundred followed the next month.

The player

Maxwell's Test career was short and sparse: seven matches between 2013 and 2017, in which he made 339 runs at 26.08 and took eight wickets at 42.62. On debut, at Hyderabad in 2013, he took 4 for 127. His big Test day came in India in 2017, when he made 104, which made him only the second Australian man with a hundred in all three international formats.

The shorter game was where he lived. He won the 50-over World Cup with Australia in 2015 and 2023 and the T20 World Cup in 2021. At the 2023 tournament he made a hundred from 40 balls against the Netherlands, at the time the fastest in World Cup history. A few weeks later, against Afghanistan in Mumbai, he arrived with Australia 91 for 7 chasing 292 and finished on 201 not out, barely able to run, sharing an unbroken stand of 202 with Pat Cummins, who made 12 of them.

What made him special

Imagination, mostly. Reverse sweeps and unorthodox pulls made him a nightmare to set a field for, because there was always a gap he had thought of first. In domestic cricket he could bat long too, with 278 for Victoria against New South Wales in 2017.

The flip side of a batter who tries everything is that not every try comes off, and selectors sometimes wished for a little more method to go with the magic. His off-spin and quick fielding meant he usually earned his place anyway.

Away from the middle

Cricket Australia named him its one-day international player of 2016 and its T20 international player in 2016 and 2019. In the Big Bash he played for the Melbourne Renegades and then the Melbourne Stars, for whom he made 154 not out against the Hobart Hurricanes in 2021–22, and turned out for several IPL sides and a string of English counties. He retired from one-day internationals in June 2025 and from all international cricket in November 2026. He supports St Kilda in the AFL.

And finally

Cricket is usually a game for people who can run between the wickets. Maxwell spent one famous evening in Mumbai showing that, with enough boundaries, it is also a game for people who cannot.
